name: RockHeron
author: miotix

sections.description:
Your ad platform counts its own results. RockHeron counts them on your site, and
puts the two numbers next to each other.

It records which campaign introduced every form submission and every WooCommerce
order, in your own database, on your own hosting. Then it shows what the platform
claimed beside what your site actually recorded, so you can see the gap rather
than take a dashboard’s word for it.

Lead source attribution

  • First touch attribution: the campaign that introduced a visitor is remembered for thirty days, and the first one keeps the credit
  • Source, medium, campaign, term and content, plus which parameter identified them
  • Six form plugins: Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms, Fluent Forms and WooCommerce
  • WooCommerce orders, read from WooCommerce’s own order attribution rather than collecting a second copy
  • A leads table showing every submission and the campaign behind it
  • Results broken down by source, medium and campaign

What else it records on your site

  • Visits, visitors and page views, with the previous period next to every number
  • Goals: calls, emails, WhatsApp clicks, form sends, add to cart, or any element you name
  • Clicks on any element you choose, by CSS selector, on all pages or only the ones you pick
  • Elements seen on screen, video plays, scroll depth, outbound clicks, downloads, site searches
  • Where visits come from: search, AI assistants, social, referral, campaigns, direct
  • Devices, browsers, operating systems, countries, landing pages, top pages
  • A live count of visitors in the last thirty minutes

Google data next to it

  • Google Site Kit is used automatically when it is installed, so you do not connect Google twice
  • No Site Kit? Connect Analytics 4 directly with your own Google Cloud OAuth client
  • Search Console clicks, impressions, CTR and average position when Site Kit is present
  • Import past months from Google Analytics so the dashboard is not empty on day one
  • Import sixteen months of Search Console history with one button when Site Kit is connected, or from the export file when it is not
  • Export any period as CSV or PDF, with the caveats carried into the file

Privacy

  • No cookies are set for analytics, and no IP address is ever stored
  • The one cookie RockHeron does set is first party and holds campaign details only: no name, no email address, no telephone number, nothing anybody typed into your form, and no advertising click identifier
  • Visitors are counted with a one way hash that changes every day
  • Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are respected
  • Works with CookiePile, the WP Consent API, or any consent cookie you name
  • Raw events are cleared on your own retention schedule while daily totals keep the history

Languages

Fully translated into Hebrew, with a right to left layout. The translation is
delivered by WordPress.org as a language pack rather than bundled in this zip,
which is why languages/ holds only the POT file: a bundled catalog would
shadow the pack and stop you receiving corrections. Any other language can be
added from that POT file, or contributed at
https://translate.wordpress.org/projects/wp-plugins/rockheron/

External services

RockHeron contacts nothing on its own. Every connection below happens only
because you connected an account or switched a setting on, and each is listed
with what is sent and when.

Google OAuth, Analytics 4 and Google Ads (optional, off until you connect them)

If you choose to connect Google directly, with your own Google Cloud OAuth
client, the plugin talks to Google from your server to read your own reports:

  • accounts.google.com – where your browser goes to approve the connection. Nothing is sent there by the plugin; you sign in to Google yourself.
  • oauth2.googleapis.com – exchanges the approval for an access token and refreshes it later. Sends your own OAuth client ID, client secret and the token.
  • analyticsdata.googleapis.com and analyticsadmin.googleapis.com – reads your Analytics 4 reports and property list. Sends the access token, the property ID and the date range and dimensions being requested.
  • googleads.googleapis.com – reads campaign spend and clicks, and only when you have entered a Google Ads customer ID and a Google approved developer token. Sends the access token, the developer token and the customer ID.

These four read your figures in. Nothing the plugin recorded about your
visitors or your leads is sent out through them: no visit, no lead, no form
entry, no email address, no name, no IP address. That is a statement about
these four connections only, and not about the Google tag below, which is a
different thing and does send visitor data to Google.

If you use Google Site Kit instead, RockHeron reads the data through Site Kit
on your own site and makes no connection of its own.

Google tag (optional, off by default, and it does send visitor data to Google)

This one runs in your visitors’ browsers, not on your server, and it is the
ordinary Google tag. Switch on “Inject the Google tag”, enter a measurement ID,
and every page your visitors load fetches
https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js and reports to Google on their
behalf.

What Google receives is what the Google tag always receives, which is visitor
data: the page being viewed and its title, the referring page, the visitor’s IP
address, their device, browser, operating system and screen size, their
approximate location derived from that IP address, and whatever Google’s own
cookies on that browser already identify. RockHeron does not choose or limit
any of it. It places the tag and Google does the rest.

Because of that:

  • It is off by default and nothing is requested from Google until you turn it on.
  • It is skipped entirely when Site Kit or another plugin is already tagging the same property, so nobody is double counted.
  • It is not loaded until the visitor has allowed it. Consent and Do Not Track are evaluated in the visitor’s own browser, not on your server, so a cached page cannot serve one visitor’s answer to the next. If you have set a consent mode, no request reaches Google before that visitor consents; if they consent later on the same page, the tag loads then.
  • Turning it on is a decision about your visitors’ data, not just your own reporting, and your privacy policy should say so.

These are Google services, governed by the Google Privacy Policy
(https://policies.google.com/privacy) and the Google APIs Terms of Service
(https://developers.google.com/terms). Analytics data handling is additionally
covered by the Google Analytics terms
(https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/).

Nothing else

RockHeron contacts no service of ours, phones no home, and loads no script or
stylesheet from a CDN. Everything it ships runs from your own server, including
the charting library below, which is bundled rather than fetched.

Third party credits

Chart.js 4.6.1, MIT licensed, bundled at assets/vendor/chartjs/. The
dashboard and report charts are drawn with it. Its license is in
assets/vendor/chartjs/LICENSE.md and the source is at
https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js/tree/v4.6.1

Nothing else is bundled.

Configuration guide

Everything below is in the plugin. Nothing here needs an account anywhere
unless you choose to connect Google.

First run, and the three screens you will use

  1. Activate the plugin and open RockHeron. Recording starts immediately and
    the first visits appear within a minute. There is nothing to switch on.
  2. RockHeron, Dashboard is traffic: sessions, daily visitors, page views,
    goal completions and conversion rate, each against the previous period, with
    cards for where visits came from, top pages and traffic over time.
  3. RockHeron, Leads is the point of the plugin: every form submission and
    WooCommerce order with the campaign that introduced the person, read as first
    touch. A result nobody could attribute is listed as Not known rather than
    dropped, so these totals never quietly disagree with your form plugin.
  4. RockHeron, Tracked elements counts anything you name with a CSS selector:
    a quote button, a telephone link, a PDF download. Tick “count this as a goal”
    and it feeds the conversion figures.
  5. RockHeron, Settings is where Google, privacy, retention and the Google
    tag live.

Form plugins are read automatically, never written to. Contact Form 7, WPForms,
Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms, Fluent Forms and WooCommerce are supported, and
the Leads screen lists which of them it can see, so an empty screen tells you
why it is empty. Both the classic and the block WooCommerce checkout are
covered.

Google: what it is for, and what you need

You do not need Google at all. The plugin records visits and leads from
your own site, in your own database. Connecting Google only adds Google’s own
numbers beside yours.

If you want them, there are three separate things, and they are independent:

  • Google Analytics 4 reporting. Settings, Google data. Either install Site
    Kit by Google and RockHeron uses its connection, or connect directly. A
    direct connection needs a Google Cloud project with the Analytics Data API
    enabled and an OAuth client of type Web application, whose Client ID and
    Client secret you paste into Settings. The scope requested is
    analytics.readonly, which is read only: nothing is written back and no
    visitor data is sent on this connection.
  • Google Ads. Only if you switch it on, which adds the adwords scope to
    the same connection so spend and clicks can be read.
  • Search Console history. No API and no credentials. Open Search Console,
    export the Performance report, and upload the zip, or the CSV files from
    inside it, in Settings. That is the whole of it.

The Google tag is a separate thing again and is off until you enter a
measurement ID. It is the ordinary gtag.js, so switching it on sends Google
what the Google tag always sends: page views, device and IP address, under
Google’s terms rather than ours. The reporting connections above send Google
nothing. Leave the field empty and no Google tag is loaded.

Campaign CSV format (Pro)

Campaigns, Add or edit campaigns takes one row per campaign. Column order does
not matter and headings are matched in English or Hebrew. Recognized columns:

campaign, `platform`, `start`, `end`, `spend`, `impressions`, `reach`,
clicks, `results`

Dates are YYYY-MM-DD. platform is one of Meta, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok
or Other. Only campaign is required; anything missing is left empty rather
than guessed. What the platform claimed is never reconciled against what your
site recorded: both are shown, and the gap between them is the number worth
looking at.

Consent, and Do Not Track

Settings, Privacy. Consent mode is off by default, which records every
visit. The other three modes are:

  • WP Consent API, for any consent plugin that implements it. Statistics
    consent is required before anything is recorded.
  • CookiePile, which is read directly.
  • A cookie you name, for anything else: give the cookie name and the value
    that means consent was given.

Where a mode is selected but cannot be evaluated, for example the consent
plugin has been deactivated, the plugin fails closed and records nothing.

Consent and Do Not Track are evaluated in the visitor’s browser, not on the
server, because a consent decision made in PHP is written into your page cache
and then served to the next visitor, whose answer may be the opposite. Respect
Do Not Track is a separate switch in the same panel. Somebody who accepts after
the page has loaded is picked up without a reload.

What is stored, how long, and how to delete it

What is kept about a lead is the campaign and a pointer to the form plugin’s
own entry. No name, no email address, no telephone number, and no advertising
click identifier. Your form plugin already holds the submission; a second copy
of every lead on your site is a duty rather than a feature.

Three retention settings, all in Settings, Stored data:

  • Attribution window, default 30 days. How long the first touch campaign is
    remembered in one first party cookie. 1 to 365.
  • Raw events, default 90 days. Individual page views are pruned nightly
    after this; the daily totals they roll up into are kept.
  • Leads, default 400 days. 30 to 3650.

To remove everything: Settings, Stored data has a tool to delete recorded data
without uninstalling. Uninstalling with “delete my data” switched on drops every
table, option, transient and scheduled job the plugin created, found by prefix
rather than from a list. Deactivating alone removes nothing except the scheduled
jobs, so your data survives an update.

How the lists are stored

Every list on the dashboard, such as top pages, referrers, campaigns and
landing pages, is rolled up once a day. Each day keeps its busiest rows by name
and sums everything else into a single “everything else” figure, so the stored
rows always account for the whole day even when the list is long.

The totals are right either way. What a cap changes is only how much of the
long tail is broken out by name: a page that ranks below the cap every day of a
range is counted, but inside that one figure rather than under its own address.

The default is 200 rows a day for pages and landing paths, 100 for referrers,
campaigns, outbound links and site searches, and 50 for the lists that cannot
produce more than that anyway, such as device, browser and country.
Settings, Stored data has one field, “Rows kept per list, per day”, that sets
a single number for every list. Zero, the default, leaves each list on its own
default. The rockheron_dim_limit filter takes ( $limit, $dim ) if you want
to raise one list without raising the rest.

Each extra row is kept for good, because the daily totals outlive the raw events
they came from. Raising this on a site with thousands of URLs costs table rows
for every day the site runs, which is why it is a setting and not simply a
larger number.

Troubleshooting

  • The dashboard is empty. The plugin only knows what it has recorded since
    it was activated; it cannot see the past. Check you are not logged in as an
    administrator or editor: those roles are excluded from recording by default,
    in Settings, What to record, so browsing your own site while logged in
    deliberately records nothing.
  • Nothing appears on a cached site. Recording runs in the browser and does
    not need the page to be uncached. If you see nothing at all, check that your
    caching or optimization plugin is not deferring or stripping the script.
  • Leads are missing. The Leads screen lists the form plugins it can see. If
    yours is not listed it is not supported yet. If it is listed but entries are
    not arriving, confirm the form actually completes: a submission that fails
    validation is not a lead.
  • Google numbers will not load. Reconnect in Settings, Google data. A
    connection that …
sections.installation:
1. Upload the plugin folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or install the zip from Plugins, Add New.
  2. Activate it.
  3. Open RockHeron. Visits start appearing within a minute.
  4. Optional: open Settings to connect Google, or install Site Kit and it is picked up on its own.
sections.faq:
Do I need Google Analytics for this to work?

No. Everything on the dashboard except the GA4, Search Console and Ads cards comes from your own site.

Will it slow my site down?

The tracking script is roughly 6 KB, loads in the footer, and sends one small beacon per page view. Reports read a pre built daily table rather than scanning raw rows.

Does it work with caching plugins?

Yes. Page views are counted in the browser, so a cached page is still recorded.

The dashboard is empty, where is my history?

The plugin starts recording the day you install it. Open Settings, Import
history from Google Analytics, and it fills the earlier months from your GA4
property. Imported days are dashed on the chart because Google counts sessions
slightly differently.

I took the site over and the old analytics account is not mine

Import your Search Console history instead. Settings, Import search history from
Search Console, upload the export file. It needs no Google connection, because
the site owner always has their own Search Console property even when the
analytics account belongs to a previous agency.

How do I track a specific button?

Open RockHeron, Tracked elements. Give it a name, paste the button’s CSS selector, and tick “count this as a goal” if it matters commercially.
sections.changelog:
1.0.0

  • Agency rollups could report a period you did not ask for, and show it as though you had. A rollup asks each site on the list for its figures and totals what comes back. It asked by range name, not by dates, and a custom period has no name to send: the other site heard nothing, answered with its own last 28 days, and those figures were totaled and displayed under the dates you chose. Two sites in different timezones had the same problem on a named range, because each resolved it against its own clock. Nothing on the card said the period was different, because figures carry no dates once they are on it, and the wrong answer was cached for fifteen minutes under the key for the right one. The figures looked entirely normal, which is the whole difficulty: an agency could send a client a report covering dates it did not cover.
  • The dates are now sent as dates. The receiving site uses the ones it is given rather than working its own out, refuses anything that is not a pair of real dates in the right order, and returns the period it answered for. The asking site checks that what came back covers exactly what it asked for, and if it does not, that site is left out of the total and named, with both periods shown, rather than quietly folded in. The check happens before the cache, so a wrong answer is never stored under the right key.
  • Exporting while looking at a custom period could give you a different period. The dashboard and the API can both be asked for any pair of dates, but the CSV and the printable report could only be asked for one of the named periods, and an unrecognized period was answered with the last 28 days rather than with a complaint. So a custom period could be exported as 28 days, named with the 28 day dates, and sent to somebody. Both now carry the dates, and a period neither recognizes is refused instead of being quietly swapped. Nobody could reach this from the dashboard, which offers only the named periods, and it is fixed before anybody could.
  • Every list is now stored complete. Lists like top pages and referrers keep their busiest rows for each day by name, and until now everything past that point was simply dropped. So a page that sat just below the line every day of a month was counted nowhere, and nothing said so: the figures were right at the top of the list and quietly short further down. Each day now also stores one “everything else” figure holding the rest, so the stored rows add up to the whole day whatever the cap. The lists themselves look the same, because that figure is never ranked among the named rows.
  • How many rows each list keeps is now yours to set, in Settings, Stored data, instead of being fixed in the code. It was 50 for every list, which is more than device or country can ever produce and too few for the pages of a real site. The defaults are now chosen per list, 200 a day for pages and landing paths and 100 for referrers and campaigns, and one field sets a single number for all of them. Bear in mind that each extra row is kept for good, since the daily totals outlive the raw events behind them.
  • First public release on WordPress.org.

0.9.9

  • The protection added in 0.9.8 could be undone by the first clearing of old events after updating, and the way to trigger it was to lengthen your retention. 0.9.8 learned how far back your raw data is still complete and refused to rebuild past it, writing that boundary down whenever events were cleared. On a site updating from an earlier version there was nothing written down yet, so the boundary had to be worked out from the data. It was, correctly, when rebuilding. It was not when clearing: that step recorded the new cutoff on its own. Clear at 90 days on the old version, update, raise retention to 180 days and clear again, and the stored boundary landed 90 days behind the truth. Everything in that gap had already been cleared by the earlier run, so the next rebuild emptied all of it, which is the fault 0.9.8 was released to stop.
  • Clearing events now works out the boundary already in force before it deletes anything, and keeps whichever is later, that or the new cutoff. It is resolved first because the surviving raw rows are the only thing that knows where the last clearing stopped, and deleting them takes that knowledge with it. It also writes a worked-out boundary down the first time it sees one, so the site stops having to infer it. The boundary can still only ever move forward.
  • Anything already worked out earlier in the same request is discarded before clearing, rather than reused. A boundary worked out from rows that have since gone reads as “nothing to protect”, which is the most expensive thing it could be wrong about.

0.9.8

  • Rebuilding the daily totals could destroy the history it was meant to rebuild. The daily table is what keeps your history after raw events pass the retention window and are cleared: that is the whole point of it. But the rebuild worked by reading the raw events for a date and writing what it found, and clearing whatever that date no longer produced. Run it over a date whose raw events had already been cleared and it found nothing, so it wrote zeros over the real figures and deleted the rest. The rebuild runs from the Settings screen, from the REST maintenance tool, and the second one is reachable by anything automating the site, so this could be set off without anybody watching. There was no warning and no way back: the rows it overwrote were the only copy left.
  • RockHeron now knows how far back its raw data is still complete, and refuses to rebuild past it. The boundary is written down whenever events are cleared, and for a site that cleared them under an earlier version it is worked out from the oldest raw row still present. The check sits in the one place every rebuild goes through, so the Settings screen, the REST tool, the hourly task and the dashboard’s own refresh are all covered by it. Dates behind the boundary are left exactly as they are.
  • The rebuild now tells you what it did not do. It reports how many days it rebuilt, how many earlier days it left alone, and the date your raw data is complete from, rather than reporting a number that quietly means something else. Clearing events past retention says the same thing: from that point those earlier days cannot be rebuilt, because there is nothing left to rebuild them from.

0.9.7

  • Accepting a consent banner started the measurement straight away on some sites and not on others, and the difference was invisible. The shared consent module listened for the events CookiePile and the WP Consent API announce an answer with. The custom consent cookie option announces nothing: the visitor accepts, some other plugin writes its cookie, and nothing tells us. So on those sites the page view the visitor had just consented to was never recorded, and with it went the campaign that introduced them, which on a single page visit is the entire record of that lead. The module now also watches the cookie itself for the two cookie based modes, which is the only way to see a cookie appear. It is a string comparison once a second, it does nothing at all while the tab is in the background, and it stops the moment the answer becomes yes. The other two modes start no timer, because they have an event.
  • The browser and the server disagreed about consent values. The server compared the cookie’s value without regard to case and the browser compared it exactly, so a consent plugin writing YES where the setting said yes was accepted by one and refused by the other: the server would have stored a visit the browser never sent. Both are case insensitive now, which is what the server always did.

0.9.6

  • The admin menu sat above everything in WordPress. RockHeron registered its top level item at position 3, which is directly under Dashboard and above Posts, so it came ahead of every core screen and every other plugin. WordPress’s admin order is something people navigate by habit and a plugin that inserts itself at the top of it is taking attention rather than earning it. It now sits at 100, below Settings. The screens and their addresses are unchanged, so existing bookmarks still work.
  • Translations are loaded only where there is a catalog to load. The plugin called load_plugin_textdomain() on every request, at plugin load time. On WordPress.org that call does nothing useful: since WordPress 4.6 the directory serves the Hebrew catalog as a language pack and core loads it against the plugin slug by itself, which is why the directory build ships only the POT file. Asking for translations that early is also how a plugin triggers the notice about loading a text domain too soon. The call is now made on init, and only when a catalog for the current locale is actually sat in the plugin, which is the case for the Pro and marketplace builds that bundle one and never the case for the directory build. Hebrew is unaffected on every channel.

0.9.5

  • The built in tracker started measuring before the visitor had answered the consent banner. Consent was checked on the server, so no visit was stored without it, but the script itself ran on page load regardless: it wrote a session id into the browser’s session storage and sent the page view, and then every click, to your own endpoint, where each one was discarded. The part you could see was what happened next. Somebody who accepted afterwards was not measured at all, because their page view had already been sent and thrown away and nothing sent it again. The tracker now asks the shared consent module before it stores or sends anything, and WordPress loads that module first because the tracker declares it as a dependency. It is also given the whole consent configuration rather than the mode alone, so the name a cookie mode is pointed at can actually be read in the browser instead of the mode denying everything by default. On acceptance the tracker starts and records the page the visitor is standing on, exactly once, with the time on page counted from that moment rather than from the banner. Consent is asked again before every send, so withdrawing it part way through a visit stops the measurement there. With no module to ask, nothing is measured. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are now read in the one shared place instead of a second copy here that could drift away from it. The server side checks are unchanged.

0.9.4

  • A configuration guide is bundled with the plugin. The readme told you how to install it and then stopped, so anything beyond the first five minutes meant guessing or asking. There is now a Configuration guide section covering the screens and what each is for, what Google is and is not used for and exactly which credentials a direct connection needs, the campaign CSV columns, how consent and Do Not Track are evaluated and what happens when a consent plugin disappears, what is stored and the three retention settings that control it, how to delete everything with and without uninstalling, the common reasons a dashboard looks empty, and where to get support.

0.9.3

  • A visitor could put a formula in your spreadsheet. A search term, a campaign name, a page title and a referrer are all written by somebody else, and a CSV cell that opens with =, +, – or @ is treated as a formula by Excel, LibreOffice and Sheets. Somebody searching your site for =1+1 had that evaluated when you opened the export, and the same opening is how a cell reaches out to a URL. Every cell is now made inert at the one point rows are written. Numbers are still numbers, so a negative figure stays a figure and the totals still add up.
  • Deactivating left a scheduled job armed. Deactivation cleared two cron events by name, and any other event this plugin had registered stayed in WordPress’s schedule and went on firing against a plugin that was no longer running. Deactivation now clears every event this plugin owns, found by name prefix rather than from a list, which is the same correction the uninstaller had. Your settings and your recorded data are untouched, so switching the plugin back on restores the schedule.

0.9.2

  • Contact Form 7 with Flamingo: the lead could be linked to somebody else’s message, and a second lead could be dropped. 0.9.1 found Flamingo’s record by reading back the newest one and accepting it if it was written in the last minute. That is guessing by recency: two people submitting within the same minute are handed the same record, which both mislinks the lead and collides on the key that keeps one submission from being written twice, so the second lead is refused. It reintroduced, in a narrower window, the bug 0.9.1 was written to fix. The link is gone and every submission gets its own identifier for the life of its request. Linking to Flamingo properly means hooking Flamingo’s own save and matching the record to the submission, not guessing, and that is not written yet. A lead with no link beats a lead pointing at a stranger’s message.
  • Chart.js is credited. The charts are drawn with Chart.js 4.6.1, MIT licensed, bundled in the plugin, and the readme said the charts were our own code and used no third party library. A new Third party credits section names it, its license and its source.
  • Screens called themselves Analytics. The menu has been called RockHeron since 0.8.0, but the dashboard’s own heading, the settings heading and the admin bar link were never carried over, so the sidebar said one thing and the page it opened said another. The readme repeated the old name too. All of them say RockHeron now.
  • The dashboard sat blank while it loaded. The headline figures, the cards and the first run panel are all drawn in the browser, and until they arrived the page reserved their height and showed nothing in it, which on a slow host reads as a broken screen rather than a loading one. Each of those areas now shows the shape of what is coming.
  • The readme said this build ships with the Hebrew translation. It ships the POT file; WordPress.org delivers Hebrew as a language pack, and a bundled catalog would shadow the pack and stop corrections reaching you. Said properly now, with a link to the translation project.
  • The changelog had two entries numbered 0.7.0. The fork note has been folded into the real one.
  • Upgrade notices for 0.9.1 and 0.9.2.

0.9.1

  • Contact Form 7 leads were being lost. Every submission of one form was recorded under the same identifier, CF7’s unit_tag, which names the form’s place on the page rather than the submission. Leads carry a unique key so that a form plugin firing its hook twice cannot write the lead twice, and that key was refusing the second visitor and everybody after them. Each submission now gets its own identifier: Flamingo’s record id where Flamingo is storing the entry, so the lead links to something real, and otherwise an identifier held for the rest of that one request, which keeps the double-fire protection without treating two people as one.
  • WooCommerce block checkout orders were never attributed. Only the classic checkout was listened for, and the block checkout goes through the Store API and fires its own hook and nothing else. It is the default on a new store, so on a new store none of the orders were attributed. Both checkouts now land in the same recording path, and the order id is still the key, so an order cannot be recorded twice.
  • The Google tag was gated on the server. Whether a visitor had consented was decided in PHP, and the answer was then written into the cached page and served to the next visitor. On a cached site, warming the cache with somebody who consented served Google’s tag to everybody who refused, and warming it with a refusal stopped the tag loading for anybody. Consent and Do Not Track are now evaluated in the visitor’s own browser, which is where they were already evaluated for the attribution cookie, and the tag also loads for somebody who accepts after the page has loaded instead of making them reload.
  • One consent evaluator instead of three. The rules existed in PHP, in the attribution script and, by implication, in the Google tag gating. They are in one file that both scripts load.
  • The external services section promised that nothing about your visitors is ever sent to Google, which was true of the four reporting connections and not true of the Google tag, which sends Google exactly what the Google tag always sends. The two are now described separately, what the tag sends is listed, the consent requirement is stated, and the settings screen says it too at the point you switch it on.

0.9.0

  • Lead sources. When somebody arrives from a tagged link, an advert or a newsletter, RockHeron keeps the campaign in one first-party cookie for thirty days, and if that visitor later submits a form or places an order the campaign is recorded next to a reference to their submission. First touch, so the campaign that introduced somebody keeps the credit rather than whatever they last clicked.
  • What is recorded is the campaign and a pointer to the form plugin’s own entry. No name, no email address, no telephone number, and no advertising click identifier. The form plugin already holds the submission and a second copy of every lead on the site is a duty rather than a feature.
  • A click identifier fills in a source the advertiser forgot to tag, and the screen says it was inferred rather than declared. A Google click identifier only ever rides on a click on a Google advert, so it reads as paid. A Facebook one is added to any outbound link including an ordinary shared post, so it reads as a referral: calling it paid would invent advertising that never happened.
  • A result nobody could attribute is recorded as unknown rather than dropped, so the totals here cannot quietly disagree with the form plugin’s own count.
  • Consent and Do Not Track are evaluated in the browser rather than on the server, because a consent decision made in PHP is written into the page cache and then served to the next visitor, whose answer may be the opposite.
  • Six form plugins are read: Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms, Fluent Forms and WooCommerce. Read, never written to: this plugin does not touch another plugin’s entries, options or settings.
  • A Leads screen showing results by source, medium, campaign and channel, with every count stating what it covers. A result with no source is drawn as Not known rather than left out, because a count that silently excludes things reads as a bug even when the exclusion is correct.
  • WooCommerce orders use the same first touch reading as forms, so an order and an inquiry are measured the same way. WooCommerce’s own order attribution is read only as a fallback for a shopper who arrived before this was switched on, and the row says so rather than passing last click off as first touch.
  • The screen lists which supported form plugins are present and which are being listened to, so an empty screen says why it is empty.

0.8.0

  • Renamed every identifier to carry the full plugin slug. The directory runs a prefix scan over functions, classes, defines, options, transients, hooks and script handles, and rejects two and three letter abbreviations, so the short prefix the fork shipped with would have cost a rename release in the middle of review.
  • Assets are versioned by their own modification time rather than the plugin version, so a browser holding the old stylesheet stops serving it after an update.
  • Author URI now points at the wordpress.org profile. A plugin whose Plugin URI and Author URI are identical is rejected at upload.
  • The free and paid co-activation guard is in place, inert until the licensing SDK is wired in.

0.7.1

  • The heron in the admin menu now takes its color from whichever admin color scheme the reader uses. WordPress ships nine and three of them are light, so no single color is right: a white mark disappears on Light and a dark one disappears on the default, and WordPress only ever varies a menu icon’s opacity, never its color. The mark is used as a mask instead and colored with currentColor, so hover, focus and current states follow by themselves, and so will any scheme added later. A plain image is still registered and shows unchanged on a browser with no mask support, or if the stylesheet does not load.

0.7.0

  • Campaigns have a screen of their own, reached from the tabs. The dashboard follows a date picker and a campaign does not: it has its own start and end, and reporting one inside the other meant either cutting figures down to a window the platform never reported or apologizing for them in a footnote. Each campaign is now reported over its own dates, with the steps from times shown through to the results the platform claims, what the money bought per thousand views, per click and per claimed result, the platform’s count beside this site’s own with the gap between them, and the site’s results per day across the campaign.
  • Campaigns that ran over the same days are reported as one piece of spending. Keeping them apart would count the same registrations against each of them and adding those up would double the site’s own results. Nothing can tell which of two simultaneous campaigns a result came from, so the screen does not pretend otherwise.
  • No spend line is drawn per day. An advertising platform reports one total for a campaign and nothing per day, and dividing that total across its days would draw a straight line that looks exactly as certain as a measured one.
  • Reach is never added up across campaigns, for the same reason it never was in the tiles: the same person reached twice is one person.
  • The three campaign figures and the campaigns table have moved off the dashboard to the new screen. Nothing was lost, and the whole period apology that used to sit under the spend figure is gone with them.
  • The currency symbol is set smaller and in the accent color, and sits beside the number rather than being pushed to the end of a Hebrew line.
  • Renamed to RockHeron, forked from WP Analytics Dash rather than renamed in place so an existing install on a live site was never touched. New prefix, text domain, option keys and tables throughout, so the two can sit side by side without colliding.

0.6.5

  • Hebrew sites now write ש”ח rather than ₪. Both are correct, but the written form is what people read in reports here, and anyone who prefers the glyph can type it into Settings.
  • The dashboard works out its own figures in the browser, and it was placing the symbol in front with nothing between, so the shekel figure read ש”ח7,528.24 there while the same figure read correctly in a printed report. The browser is now handed the arrangement PHP already decided instead of guessing at it again.

0.6.4

  • Money carries its currency. It used to appear bare unless WooCommerce was installed, so a campaign costing 7,528 shekels read as 7,528 of nothing. The symbol now follows WooCommerce, then your site language, and you can set it yourself in Settings. A glyph sits against the figure and letters stand apart from it, because 100 ש”ח and ₪100 are both right and running either together is not.

0.6.3

  • The change under each KPI sat on the left in Hebrew. It is a flex row, so the alignment it was given did nothing: its arrow and figure are placed by justify-content, and because the box is forced left to right so that a minus sign stays on the left of the number, the default end was the wrong one.
  • A figure that becomes available after you last chose your tiles now appears. A saved selection is a list of what to show, so anything invented or connected later was simply absent from it, which looks exactly like having been switched off. Enter a campaign and its cost per result would never have shown up, with nothing on screen to explain why. Figures you deliberately removed stay removed.

0.6.2

  • The new campaigns card was given an id that an existing card already used, so PHP kept one definition and the other code went on answering, and the card showed the wrong table with no rows. Renamed, and the static check now reports a duplicate key in any array literal.
  • A card whose source is not connected yet is no longer written into your layout as switched off. It was not offered in the chooser, so it was never a choice you made, and it would have stayed hidden on the day the source finally arrived.

0.6.1

  • Fixes a fatal error on the settings screen in 0.6.0. The two new panels were called from inside another section, where the variable they needed did not exist, so the page stopped rendering half way down and the panels never appeared.
  • The static check now reports a variable read before anything in its own function could have defined it, which is the mistake above. Every other check passed on that code: the class resolved, the method existed, the settings key was real.
  • Imported search history tops itself up every night instead of freezing on the day it was imported. The window is wider than Google’s reporting lag on purpose, because Search Console revises a day for a while after first reporting it.
  • KPI figures sit under their labels again in Hebrew. Forcing them to left to right so a minus sign stays on the left of the number also pushed them to the left of their tile.

0.6.0

  • Campaigns. Record what an advertising platform says a campaign did and the dashboard keeps it next to what this site actually recorded over the same dates. The two are never reconciled and neither corrects the other: a platform only counts a result it believes its own ad caused, and a site only counts what reached its database. The gap between them is usually the most interesting number on the page and it is invisible in either system alone.
  • Add campaigns by hand or import a CSV. Column order does not matter and the headings are matched in English or Hebrew, because the file usually arrives exported by somebody who will not be asked to redo it.
  • Reach and frequency are held per campaign and never added up across campaigns, because two campaigns may have reached the same people and nothing here can tell.
  • Point the dashboard at where your results actually live. Most sites were recording registrations or inquiries in a form plugin or a custom post type long before any analytics arrived, and that is the number the business cares about. Pick the post type in Settings and it gets counted, including from dates before this plugin existed. Developers can register any other source with the rockheron_goal_sources filter.
  • Trashed entries count by default, because on most sites the trash is where declined and duplicate submissions go, and a declined submission still happened. Leaving it out quietly makes the marketing look worse than it was.
  • A figure with nothing to compare against no longer claims to be new every time it is shown.

0.5.1

  • The report is a designed document now, with a masthead, the charts, and the numbers behind each one. It had been a bare stack of tables.
  • Other plugins’ notices no longer print into it. They were being removed by stylesheet, which only works for the ones you can name, so they are now removed at the source on that screen and anything else in the page is taken out of the printed flow by position rather than by class.
  • Charts print in color, headings repeat on every page, and nothing breaks in the middle of a row or a tile.
  • A signed number no longer loses its sign to the other end of the line in Hebrew. The bidi algorithm treats a leading plus or minus as neutral, so -7.7% was being shown as 7.7%-, which reads as a different number.
  • Donut legends sit under the ring on a narrow chart instead of beside it, where the labels were …

short_description: See where your leads actually came from, and whether the ad platform's numbers match what your site recorded.
description:
Your ad platform counts its own results. RockHeron counts them on your site, and
puts the two numbers next to each other.

It records which campaign introduced every form submission and every WooCommerce
order, in your own database, on your own hosting. Then it shows what the platform
claimed beside what your site actually recorded, so you can see the gap rather
than take a dashboard’s word for it.

Lead source attribution

  • First touch attribution: the campaign that introduced a visitor is remembered for thirty days, and the first one keeps the credit
  • Source, medium, campaign, term and content, plus which parameter identified them
  • Six form plugins: Contact Form 7, WPForms, Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms, Fluent Forms and WooCommerce
  • WooCommerce orders, read from WooCommerce’s own order attribution rather than collecting a second copy
  • A leads table showing every submission and the campaign behind it
  • Results broken down by source, medium and campaign

What else it records on your site

  • Visits, visitors and page views, with the previous period next to every number
  • Goals: calls, emails, WhatsApp clicks, form sends, add to cart, or any element you name
  • Clicks on any element you choose, by CSS selector, on all pages or only the ones you pick
  • Elements seen on screen, video plays, scroll depth, outbound clicks, downloads, site searches
  • Where visits come from: search, AI assistants, social, referral, campaigns, direct
  • Devices, browsers, operating systems, countries, landing pages, top pages
  • A live count of visitors in the last thirty minutes

Google data next to it

  • Google Site Kit is used automatically when it is installed, so you do not connect Google twice
  • No Site Kit? Connect Analytics 4 directly with your own Google Cloud OAuth client
  • Search Console clicks, impressions, CTR and average position when Site Kit is present
  • Import past months from Google Analytics so the dashboard is not empty on day one
  • Import sixteen months of Search Console history with one button when Site Kit is connected, or from the export file when it is not
  • Export any period as CSV or PDF, with the caveats carried into the file

Privacy

  • No cookies are set for analytics, and no IP address is ever stored
  • The one cookie RockHeron does set is first party and holds campaign details only: no name, no email address, no telephone number, nothing anybody typed into your form, and no advertising click identifier
  • Visitors are counted with a one way hash that changes every day
  • Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are respected
  • Works with CookiePile, the WP Consent API, or any consent cookie you name
  • Raw events are cleared on your own retention schedule while daily totals keep the history

Languages

Fully translated into Hebrew, with a right to left layout. The translation is
delivered by WordPress.org as a language pack rather than bundled in this zip,
which is why languages/ holds only the POT file: a bundled catalog would
shadow the pack and stop you receiving corrections. Any other language can be
added from that POT file, or contributed at
https://translate.wordpress.org/projects/wp-plugins/rockheron/

External services

RockHeron contacts nothing on its own. Every connection below happens only
because you connected an account or switched a setting on, and each is listed
with what is sent and when.

Google OAuth, Analytics 4 and Google Ads (optional, off until you connect them)

If you choose to connect Google directly, with your own Google Cloud OAuth
client, the plugin talks to Google from your server to read your own reports:

  • accounts.google.com – where your browser goes to approve the connection. Nothing is sent there by the plugin; you sign in to Google yourself.
  • oauth2.googleapis.com – exchanges the approval for an access token and refreshes it later. Sends your own OAuth client ID, client secret and the token.
  • analyticsdata.googleapis.com and analyticsadmin.googleapis.com – reads your Analytics 4 reports and property list. Sends the access token, the property ID and the date range and dimensions being requested.
  • googleads.googleapis.com – reads campaign spend and clicks, and only when you have entered a Google Ads customer ID and a Google approved developer token. Sends the access token, the developer token and the customer ID.

These four read your figures in. Nothing the plugin recorded about your
visitors or your leads is sent out through them: no visit, no lead, no form
entry, no email address, no name, no IP address. That is a statement about
these four connections only, and not about the Google tag below, which is a
different thing and does send visitor data to Google.

If you use Google Site Kit instead, RockHeron reads the data through Site Kit
on your own site and makes no connection of its own.

Google tag (optional, off by default, and it does send visitor data to Google)

This one runs in your visitors’ browsers, not on your server, and it is the
ordinary Google tag. Switch on “Inject the Google tag”, enter a measurement ID,
and every page your visitors load fetches
https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtag/js and reports to Google on their
behalf.

What Google receives is what the Google tag always receives, which is visitor
data: the page being viewed and its title, the referring page, the visitor’s IP
address, their device, browser, operating system and screen size, their
approximate location derived from that IP address, and whatever Google’s own
cookies on that browser already identify. RockHeron does not choose or limit
any of it. It places the tag and Google does the rest.

Because of that:

  • It is off by default and nothing is requested from Google until you turn it on.
  • It is skipped entirely when Site Kit or another plugin is already tagging the same property, so nobody is double counted.
  • It is not loaded until the visitor has allowed it. Consent and Do Not Track are evaluated in the visitor’s own browser, not on your server, so a cached page cannot serve one visitor’s answer to the next. If you have set a consent mode, no request reaches Google before that visitor consents; if they consent later on the same page, the tag loads then.
  • Turning it on is a decision about your visitors’ data, not just your own reporting, and your privacy policy should say so.

These are Google services, governed by the Google Privacy Policy
(https://policies.google.com/privacy) and the Google APIs Terms of Service
(https://developers.google.com/terms). Analytics data handling is additionally
covered by the Google Analytics terms
(https://marketingplatform.google.com/about/analytics/terms/us/).

Nothing else

RockHeron contacts no service of ours, phones no home, and loads no script or
stylesheet from a CDN. Everything it ships runs from your own server, including
the charting library below, which is bundled rather than fetched.

Third party credits

Chart.js 4.6.1, MIT licensed, bundled at assets/vendor/chartjs/. The
dashboard and report charts are drawn with it. Its license is in
assets/vendor/chartjs/LICENSE.md and the source is at
https://github.com/chartjs/Chart.js/tree/v4.6.1

Nothing else is bundled.

Configuration guide

Everything below is in the plugin. Nothing here needs an account anywhere
unless you choose to connect Google.

First run, and the three screens you will use

  1. Activate the plugin and open RockHeron. Recording starts immediately and
    the first visits appear within a minute. There is nothing to switch on.
  2. RockHeron, Dashboard is traffic: sessions, daily visitors, page views,
    goal completions and conversion rate, each against the previous period, with
    cards for where visits came from, top pages and traffic over time.
  3. RockHeron, Leads is the point of the plugin: every form submission and
    WooCommerce order with the campaign that introduced the person, read as first
    touch. A result nobody could attribute is listed as Not known rather than
    dropped, so these totals never quietly disagree with your form plugin.
  4. RockHeron, Tracked elements counts anything you name with a CSS selector:
    a quote button, a telephone link, a PDF download. Tick “count this as a goal”
    and it feeds the conversion figures.
  5. RockHeron, Settings is where Google, privacy, retention and the Google
    tag live.

Form plugins are read automatically, never written to. Contact Form 7, WPForms,
Gravity Forms, Elementor Forms, Fluent Forms and WooCommerce are supported, and
the Leads screen lists which of them it can see, so an empty screen tells you
why it is empty. Both the classic and the block WooCommerce checkout are
covered.

Google: what it is for, and what you need

You do not need Google at all. The plugin records visits and leads from
your own site, in your own database. Connecting Google only adds Google’s own
numbers beside yours.

If you want them, there are three separate things, and they are independent:

  • Google Analytics 4 reporting. Settings, Google data. Either install Site
    Kit by Google and RockHeron uses its connection, or connect directly. A
    direct connection needs a Google Cloud project with the Analytics Data API
    enabled and an OAuth client of type Web application, whose Client ID and
    Client secret you paste into Settings. The scope requested is
    analytics.readonly, which is read only: nothing is written back and no
    visitor data is sent on this connection.
  • Google Ads. Only if you switch it on, which adds the adwords scope to
    the same connection so spend and clicks can be read.
  • Search Console history. No API and no credentials. Open Search Console,
    export the Performance report, and upload the zip, or the CSV files from
    inside it, in Settings. That is the whole of it.

The Google tag is a separate thing again and is off until you enter a
measurement ID. It is the ordinary gtag.js, so switching it on sends Google
what the Google tag always sends: page views, device and IP address, under
Google’s terms rather than ours. The reporting connections above send Google
nothing. Leave the field empty and no Google tag is loaded.

Campaign CSV format (Pro)

Campaigns, Add or edit campaigns takes one row per campaign. Column order does
not matter and headings are matched in English or Hebrew. Recognized columns:

campaign, `platform`, `start`, `end`, `spend`, `impressions`, `reach`,
clicks, `results`

Dates are YYYY-MM-DD. platform is one of Meta, Google Ads, LinkedIn, TikTok
or Other. Only campaign is required; anything missing is left empty rather
than guessed. What the platform claimed is never reconciled against what your
site recorded: both are shown, and the gap between them is the number worth
looking at.

Consent, and Do Not Track

Settings, Privacy. Consent mode is off by default, which records every
visit. The other three modes are:

  • WP Consent API, for any consent plugin that implements it. Statistics
    consent is required before anything is recorded.
  • CookiePile, which is read directly.
  • A cookie you name, for anything else: give the cookie name and the value
    that means consent was given.

Where a mode is selected but cannot be evaluated, for example the consent
plugin has been deactivated, the plugin fails closed and records nothing.

Consent and Do Not Track are evaluated in the visitor’s browser, not on the
server, because a consent decision made in PHP is written into your page cache
and then served to the next visitor, whose answer may be the opposite. Respect
Do Not Track is a separate switch in the same panel. Somebody who accepts after
the page has loaded is picked up without a reload.

What is stored, how long, and how to delete it

What is kept about a lead is the campaign and a pointer to the form plugin’s
own entry. No name, no email address, no telephone number, and no advertising
click identifier. Your form plugin already holds the submission; a second copy
of every lead on your site is a duty rather than a feature.

Three retention settings, all in Settings, Stored data:

  • Attribution window, default 30 days. How long the first touch campaign is
    remembered in one first party cookie. 1 to 365.
  • Raw events, default 90 days. Individual page views are pruned nightly
    after this; the daily totals they roll up into are kept.
  • Leads, default 400 days. 30 to 3650.

To remove everything: Settings, Stored data has a tool to delete recorded data
without uninstalling. Uninstalling with “delete my data” switched on drops every
table, option, transient and scheduled job the plugin created, found by prefix
rather than from a list. Deactivating alone removes nothing except the scheduled
jobs, so your data survives an update.

How the lists are stored

Every list on the dashboard, such as top pages, referrers, campaigns and
landing pages, is rolled up once a day. Each day keeps its busiest rows by name
and sums everything else into a single “everything else” figure, so the stored
rows always account for the whole day even when the list is long.

The totals are right either way. What a cap changes is only how much of the
long tail is broken out by name: a page that ranks below the cap every day of a
range is counted, but inside that one figure rather than under its own address.

The default is 200 rows a day for pages and landing paths, 100 for referrers,
campaigns, outbound links and site searches, and 50 for the lists that cannot
produce more than that anyway, such as device, browser and country.
Settings, Stored data has one field, “Rows kept per list, per day”, that sets
a single number for every list. Zero, the default, leaves each list on its own
default. The rockheron_dim_limit filter takes ( $limit, $dim ) if you want
to raise one list without raising the rest.

Each extra row is kept for good, because the daily totals outlive the raw events
they came from. Raising this on a site with thousands of URLs costs table rows
for every day the site runs, which is why it is a setting and not simply a
larger number.

Troubleshooting

  • The dashboard is empty. The plugin only knows what it has recorded since
    it was activated; it cannot see the past. Check you are not logged in as an
    administrator or editor: those roles are excluded from recording by default,
    in Settings, What to record, so browsing your own site while logged in
    deliberately records nothing.
  • Nothing appears on a cached site. Recording runs in the browser and does
    not need the page to be uncached. If you see nothing at all, check that your
    caching or optimization plugin is not deferring or stripping the script.
  • Leads are missing. The Leads screen lists the form plugins it can see. If
    yours is not listed it is not supported yet. If it is listed but entries are
    not arriving, confirm the form actually completes: a submission that fails
    validation is not a lead.
  • Google numbers will not load. Reconnect in Settings, Google data. A
    connection that …

upgrade_notice.1.0.0: First public release. Also fixes agency rollups reporting a period you did not ask for: a custom date range could be answered with the other site's last 28 days and totaled as though it were the dates you chose. Take this if you use rollups.
upgrade_notice.0.9.9: Closes a hole in the 0.9.8 fix. If you updated from 0.9.7 or earlier and then lengthened your retention, the next clearing of old events could lose track of how far back your data was really complete, and a rebuild after that would empty the dates an earlier clearing had already emptied. Take this if you are on 0.9.8.
upgrade_notice.0.9.8: Fixes a bug that could wipe your recorded history. Rebuilding daily totals over dates whose raw events had already been cleared overwrote them with zeros, and the daily totals are the only copy of that history. Take this one.
upgrade_notice.0.9.7: Fixes consent handling for sites using a custom consent cookie, where accepting the banner did not start recording until the visitor moved to another page. Worth taking if you use that option.
upgrade_notice.0.9.6: Moves the RockHeron menu from the top of your admin sidebar to below Settings, and stops the plugin asking for translations it does not need. Nothing else changes.
upgrade_notice.0.9.5: The built in tracker no longer runs before consent is given, and a visitor who accepts after the page has loaded is now measured from that moment instead of being missed. Worth taking if you use a consent plugin or have set a consent mode.
upgrade_notice.0.9.4: Adds a full configuration guide to the bundled documentation. No code changes; there is no need to update unless you want the guide.
upgrade_notice.0.9.3: Exported CSVs can no longer carry a formula written by a visitor, and deactivating the plugin now clears every scheduled job it registered. Worth taking if you export reports or use scheduled reports.
upgrade_notice.0.9.2: Contact Form 7 leads are recorded correctly when Flamingo is active. 0.9.1 linked the lead to whichever Flamingo record was newest, which on a busy form meant the wrong message and a dropped lead. Chart.js is now credited. Upgrade if you use Contact Form 7.
upgrade_notice.0.9.1: Fixes three faults that lost data: every Contact Form 7 lead after the first was dropped, WooCommerce block checkout orders were never attributed, and the Google tag was loaded from a consent decision baked into your page cache. Upgrade.
upgrade_notice.0.7.0: Campaigns get their own screen, reported over their own dates.
upgrade_notice.0.6.5: Shekels are written ש"ח, and the dashboard places the symbol correctly.
upgrade_notice.0.6.3: New figures reach your dashboard instead of waiting to be found.
upgrade_notice.0.6.2: Fixes the campaigns card, which showed the wrong table in 0.6.0 and 0.6.1.
upgrade_notice.0.6.1: Fixes a fatal error on the settings screen in 0.6.0. Install this.
upgrade_notice.0.6.0: Campaign figures beside your own, and results counted where you keep them.
upgrade_notice.0.5.1: A properly designed PDF report, with charts.
upgrade_notice.0.5.0: CSV and PDF export of the period on screen.
upgrade_notice.0.4.4: KPI tiles are boxes, so an odd number no longer wraps badly.
upgrade_notice.0.4.3: Search clicks join the main traffic chart.
upgrade_notice.0.4.2: Unmeasured days are left blank instead of drawn as zero.
upgrade_notice.0.4.1: Adds a search over time chart for the imported history.
upgrade_notice.0.4.0: Search Console history with one button when Site Kit is connected.
upgrade_notice.0.3.2: Figures line up on their units digit in right to left layouts.
upgrade_notice.0.3.1: Correct formatting for rates and averages, and aligned numeric columns.
upgrade_notice.0.3.0: Search Console history import, no Google connection required.
upgrade_notice.0.2.0: Adds Google Analytics history import and Hebrew.
